books.section: Topic 5.9 Government Policies During the Civil War
Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Abraham Lincoln, Second Inaugural Address, March 4, 1865. Public domain. Wording verified against the Avalon Project and National Park Service texts. “. . .” marks omitted text between passages, quoted in their order in the source.
stimulus.text:
“One-eighth of the whole population were colored slaves, not distributed generally over the Union, but localized in the southern part of it. These slaves constituted a peculiar and powerful interest. All knew that this interest was somehow the cause of the war. . . . Yet, if God wills that it continue, until all the wealth piled by the bond-man’s 250 years of unrequited toil shall be sunk, and until every drop of blood drawn with the lash, shall be paid by another drawn with the sword, as was said 3,000 years ago, so still it must be said ‘the judgments of the Lord, are true and righteous altogether.’ . . . With malice toward none; with charity for all; . . . let us strive on to finish the work we are in; to bind up the nation’s wounds.”

—Abraham Lincoln, Second Inaugural Address, March 4, 1865

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Lincoln suggests the war may be God’s punishment for slavery, lasting “until every drop of blood drawn with the lash, shall be paid by another drawn with the sword.” This framing presents the war as

options.text: a holy war that the North was certain to win in the end.
options.misconception: Background: Lincoln says the war may continue until God’s purposes are served; he claims no certainty of Northern victory.

options.text: proof that God favored the Confederacy over the Union cause.
options.misconception: Background: Lincoln says both sides prayed to the same God and neither prayer was fully answered.

options.text: a moral reckoning for North and South together, not for one side alone.
a war with no deeper meaning beyond the battlefield itself.
options.misconception: Background: Lincoln gives the war deep meaning, calling slavery its cause and the war God’s reckoning for it.

rationales.A: Background: Lincoln says the war may continue until God’s purposes are served; he claims no certainty of Northern victory.
rationales.B: Background: Lincoln says both sides prayed to the same God and neither prayer was fully answered.
rationales.D: Background: Lincoln gives the war deep meaning, calling slavery its cause and the war God’s reckoning for it.
rationales.C: Lincoln says God gives the war to both North and South as the woe due to those by whom the offense of slavery came.
rationales.general:
1. Lincoln does not hand victory to one side and blame to the other.
2. He says both sides read the same Bible and prayed to the same God.
3. The blood of the lash is answered by the blood of the sword, for North and South alike.
4. Slavery is the offense, and the whole nation pays for it.
Remember: when a speech shares the blame, it is arguing for a shared peace afterward.
